name: Personal radiation dosimeters and badges
summary: Small devices worn on the chest or hand that add up a person's radiation dose: lab-read badges, pocket dosimeters with an eyepiece and electronic dosimeters.
uses: Electronic dosimeters show total dose and, on many models, dose rate, and beep, flash or vibrate at set levels; not every model shows a live rate (CNSC INFO-0827; REMM detectors)
TLD, OSL and film badges store the dose for a lab reader and show the wearer nothing, so off-grid they are useless (REMM detectors; Health Canada NDS badge)
Pocket dosimeters are read through an eyepiece but must be charged first; pocket chambers need a separate charger-reader (ORAU dosimeters; REMM detectors)
They total your own dose; to find a source or check a load, the CNSC points to a survey meter (CNSC INFO-0814)
The Mirion DMC 3000 shows dose rate only from 10 µSv/h (1 µSv/h with an extended option), far above normal background, so a blank rate there is expected (DMC 3000 datasheet)
A low or zero reading is not proof of safety: a flat battery, an uncharged pocket dosimeter or a lab-read badge shows nothing live
identify: Badges: a small plastic holder clipped to the front of the body between waist and neck, or on the hands as an extremity badge (CNSC INFO-0827). Health Canada's National Dosimetry Services badge is a royal blue rectangle with a white label giving the wearer's name, wearing dates and NDS-SND (Health Canada NDS badge). Badges are swapped every wearing period, usually 3 months (Health Canada dosimeter journey). Pocket dosimeters have an eyepiece on one end; point the other end at a light and read where the fibre sits on the scale (REMM detectors). The US civil-defence CD V-742 reads 0–200 R (ORAU CD V instruments); the CD V-750 charger was made to charge it, setting the fibre to zero (ORAU CD V-750). Electronic dosimeters: pager-sized, with a screen in µSv, mSv or mrem and alarm lights; the Mirion DMC 3000 runs on one AAA cell, measures X and gamma from 15 keV to 7 MeV, alarms at about 85 dB and meets IEC 61526 (DMC 3000 datasheet). In Canada only industrial radiographers are required to carry a direct-reading dosimeter, but many other licensees use them (CNSC INFO-0827). For scale: the public dose limit is 1 mSv a year and a nuclear energy worker's is 50 mSv a year (CNSC radiation doses).
test: Badges: there is no field test. A TLD or OSL badge gives up its dose only in a lab reader, after which it is reset (Health Canada dosimeter journey), so treat a found badge as a record of someone's job, not an instrument. Electronic: fit a fresh cell of the type marked and switch on; the DMC 3000 takes one AAA alkaline and runs about 2,500 hours continuously (DMC 3000 datasheet). Check the screen, lights and alarm all work, note the total dose, leave it running for a day and look again. Normal background is 0.05–0.2 µSv/h (CNSC INFO-0814), very roughly 1–5 µSv a day. Our own reasoning, not a maker's test: a unit that adds nothing over several days, or jumps with nothing near it, is suspect, though some models ignore very low rates. Creeping up shows only that it is alive, not that it reads right; CNSC says instruments need periodic calibration (CNSC INFO-0814), so treat uncalibrated figures as rough. Pocket dosimeters: they need their own charger, which sets the fibre to zero (ORAU CD V-750); without one a found unit can't be used. If you have one, read it each day: our own rule is that a reading that climbs with no source near can't be trusted. Early pocket chambers could discharge from a knock and fake a dose, so workers wore two and took the lower reading (ORAU dosimeters).

decay.note: Estimate. Lab-read badges are useless without a reader from day one (Health Canada dosimeter journey); a worn OSL badge can be read up to a year later (REMM detectors). Electronic and pocket units keep working while you have cells or a charger (ORAU dosimeters).

improvise: A Geiger counter or survey meter is the better tool: it shows the dose rate where you stand (CNSC INFO-0814). For a rough dose, multiply the rate by the hours spent there if it stays steady: 10 µSv/h for 5 hours is about 50 µSv. For scale, Canada's public limit is 1 mSv (1,000 µSv) in a year (CNSC radiation doses); that is a regulatory limit, not an emergency guide, so follow any official advice. With no instrument at all, keep your time near any suspected source short, stay as far away as you can, and put concrete or lead between you and it (CNSC protecting workers). Never walk toward a source to test anything: CNSC says only people trained in radiation safety should investigate unidentified radioactive material (CNSC INFO-0814), and follow the official shelter advice: go inside, away from windows, and stay put until told otherwise (Get Prepared radiological). A badge gives no reading without the lab, so don't let one give you false comfort (REMM detectors).
